lessons.title: Legal systems and cybercrime laws
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of the scales of justice resting on a big law book, next to a computer keyboard and a judge's gavel.
objectives: Tell apart common law, civil law, customary law and religious law.
Differentiate criminal law, civil law and administrative law, and their standards of proof.
Place the main American and European laws often cited in the exam.
Understand the difficulties of international investigations.

references.title: Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime (Budapest, 2001)
French Penal Code, Articles 323-1 et seq. (offenses against automated data processing systems)

blocks.text: The main families of law

rows: Judges' decisions and precedents make the law
United Kingdom, United States, Canada (outside Quebec), Australia
Written codes passed by the legislature; the judge applies them
Customs and traditions recognized as rules

blocks.text: Common law = the judge and precedent. Civil law = the code.

blocks.title: Who makes the rule?
blocks.alt: Four-cell table: in common law, the judge and their precedents; in civil law, the legislature and its codes; in customary law, custom and tradition; in religious law, religious texts.

blocks.text: The branches of law

rows: Rules set by public authorities and regulators

blocks.text: In the exam: an intrusion can lead both to criminal prosecution (against the perpetrator) and to a civil action (to compensate for the harm). The standard of proof required in criminal cases is higher than in civil cases.
Laws often cited

rows: Interception of communications in transit (Wiretap Act); its other titles cover stored communications (Stored Communications Act) and number records
Digital copyright, circumvention of technical protections
Economic Espionage Act (1996), Defend Trade Secrets Act (2016)
Reliability of the financial reporting of listed companies and internal controls
Commercial email: no misleading subject, postal address, opt-out honored within 10 business days
Fraudulent access to or remaining in a system, obstruction, alteration of data (Penal Code, Art. 323-1 et seq.)
Cybersecurity of essential and important entities

blocks.title: A standard is not a law
blocks.text: PCI DSS is a standard imposed by contract by the payment card networks, not a law. ISO standards are voluntary, unless a contract or a regulation makes them mandatory. An exam question may play on this difference.
The international puzzle

blocks.title: Why cross-border investigations are difficult
items: The attacker, the servers and the victim may fall under different countries and laws.
An act punished in one country may not be punished in another.
Collecting evidence abroad goes through mutual legal assistance, which is often slow.
The Budapest Convention harmonizes offenses and facilitates cooperation between signatory states.
Rules on data transfers limit what can be sent outside the EU.

blocks.title: Case: an intrusion from elsewhere
blocks.text: A fictitious French SME discovers that a former contractor, based in another country, kept connecting to its server after the end of the contract. Legal files a complaint in France for fraudulently remaining in a system (Godfrain Act) and, in parallel, brings a civil action to obtain compensation. The timestamped logs and the chain of custody, prepared by the CSIRT, are passed on to the investigators.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Lawyer: I determine the applicable laws according to where the events, the data and the people are.
CISO: I list the legal and contractual obligations that apply to my organization.
Investigator: I collect evidence so that it is admissible in criminal as well as civil proceedings.
Auditor: I check that each obligation has an owner and proof of compliance.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Common law = judges' precedents; civil law = codes.
Criminal = society, prison possible; civil = compensation; administrative = regulators.
ECPA = interception in transit; Stored Communications Act = stored communications.
SOX = financial reporting; HIPAA = health; GLBA = finance; FISMA = federal government.
PCI DSS is contractual, not legal.
Families of law: common law, civil, customary, religious, mixed.
Branches: criminal, civil, administrative; standards of proof.
Key laws: CFAA, ECPA, DMCA, HIPAA, GLBA, SOX, FISMA, CAN-SPAM, Godfrain, GDPR, NIS 2.
International investigations: jurisdiction, mutual assistance, Budapest Convention.

lessons.title: Intellectual property and privacy
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a light bulb protected by a small padlock, next to an identity card with a silhouette in which some lines are hidden.
objectives: Tell apart patent, copyright, trademark and trade secret.
Apply the principles of personal data protection (OECD, GDPR).
Identify controller, processor and data protection officer.
Govern data transfers outside the European Union.

references.title: OECD Guidelines on the Protection of Privacy and Transborder Flows of Personal Data (1980, revised in 2013)

blocks.text: Protecting creations

rows: A new, inventive and industrially applicable invention
The expression of a work (text, source code, image), not the idea
Life of the author + 70 years (EU, United States for most works)
The code of a piece of software
A sign that distinguishes products or services
Renewable without limit as long as it is used and renewed (10 years per period in the EU)
As long as the secret is protected

blocks.title: Four ways to protect a creation
blocks.alt: Four-cell table: a patent protects an invention for about 20 years; copyright protects the expression of a work; a trademark protects a distinctive sign and is renewed; a trade secret protects information as long as it stays secret.

cells.label: Trade secret
cells.detail: as long as it stays secret

blocks.text: Patent = invention, published in exchange for a monopoly. Trade secret = nothing is published, protection lasts as long as the secret holds.

blocks.title: Protecting a trade secret
items: Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with employees and partners.
Access control based on need to know.
Classification and labeling of documents.
Data loss prevention (DLP) and monitoring of exfiltration.
Reminder of obligations when an employee leaves.

blocks.title: Licenses and piracy
blocks.text: Using software beyond its license (number of workstations, commercial use) or copying code without respecting its license, including open source, exposes the organization to lawsuits. An inventory of software and licenses is part of compliance.
Protecting people: privacy

rows: Determines the purposes and means of processing; is accountable for compliance
Processes data on behalf of the controller, under a contract (Art. 28)
Advises, monitors compliance, contact point for the authority; mandatory in some cases (Art. 37)
Has rights: access, rectification, erasure, objection, portability…

blocks.text: Transfers outside the EU

blocks.title: Personal data transfers
blocks.text: A transfer outside the European Economic Area is only allowed if the country offers an adequate level of protection (Commission adequacy decision) or with appropriate safeguards: standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules. The EU–US Privacy Shield was invalidated in 2020 (Schrems II ruling); it was replaced in 2023 by the EU–US Data Privacy Framework.

Privacy and security complement each other: privacy cannot be protected without security, but excessive security (unlimited monitoring of employees) can infringe privacy. Minimization and proportionality guide both.

blocks.title: Case: the new analytics tool
blocks.text: A fictitious retailer wants to entrust the analysis of its customer files to a provider hosted outside the EU. The DPO checks the purpose, reduces the data to the strict minimum (no dates of birth), has a processing contract compliant with Article 28 signed, relies on standard contractual clauses and carries out a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) because the processing concerns a large number of people.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: DPO: I check purpose and minimization before any new processing.
Lawyer: I protect inventions by patent or by secrecy depending on the strategy.
CISO: I put in place the security measures that the GDPR requires to be "appropriate to the risk".
Developer: I respect the licenses of the libraries I integrate.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Copyright protects the expression, not the idea.
Patent: 20 years, publication; trade secret: no publication, unlimited duration as long as it is kept.
Controller = decides; processor = carries out.
Privacy Shield invalidated in 2020; Data Privacy Framework since 2023.
Minimization: collect only what is necessary.
Patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret.
OECD and GDPR principles.
Roles: controller, processor, DPO, data subject.
Transfers: adequacy, standard clauses, binding corporate rules.

lessons.title: Liability, compliance and ethics
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a compass whose needle points to the word "ethics", lying on a compliance checklist with ticked boxes.
objectives: Explain due care and due diligence.
Recognize negligence and liability toward third parties.
Describe the elements of an effective compliance program.
Apply ethical principles in professional decisions.

references.title: (ISC)², Code of Ethics (four canons), example of a professional code of ethics
RFC 1087, Ethics and the Internet (Internet Activities Board, 1989)

blocks.text: Care and diligence

rows: Doing what a reasonable and prudent person would do: putting the expected measures in place
Investigating, verifying and continuously checking that the measures are suitable and work

blocks.text: Due diligence = think and verify before and during. Due care = act as you should.

blocks.title: Negligence and the prudent person rule
blocks.text: An organization that does not take the measures a prudent person would have taken in the same situation can be judged negligent and liable for the damage. Executives can be held personally liable if they have not exercised due care.

blocks.title: Liability toward third parties
blocks.text: If a poorly protected system is used to attack other organizations (botnet relay, leak of a partner's data), the organization may be held liable toward those third parties. Contracts with suppliers and partners specify security obligations, audits and notifications.
A compliance program

blocks.title: Essential elements
items: A designated compliance officer, with the necessary authority and resources.
An inventory of obligations: laws, regulations, contracts, standards.
Written policies and procedures, approved by senior management.
Staff training and awareness.
Regular internal and external audits.
A reporting channel and known disciplinary rules.
Tracked corrective actions and a report to senior management.

blocks.title: The compliance loop
blocks.alt: Five-step cycle: identify the obligations, write the policies, implement and train, check and audit, correct and report, with the compliance officer at the center.

blocks.text: Professional ethics

Security professionals have access to significant information and powers. The codes of ethics of certification bodies govern their conduct; every candidate must know and respect the code of their own certification body.

rows: Example: the four canons of the (ISC)² code
Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure
Do not put the public at risk
Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally
Respect the law and tell the truth
Provide diligent and competent service to principals
Do not accept an assignment beyond your skills
Share, train, do not harm the reputation of the profession

blocks.title: Unethical behavior (based on RFC 1087)
items: Seeking to gain unauthorized access to the resources of the Internet.
Disrupting the intended use of the Internet.
Wasting resources (people, capacity, computers).
Destroying the integrity of computer-based information.
Compromising the privacy of users.

blocks.text: Faced with an exam dilemma, choose the answer that protects society and people first, that stays legal and honest, and that goes through the proper channels (management, compliance, authorities) rather than through a personal action such as a "hack back" or an unsupervised public disclosure.

blocks.title: Case: the consultant's dilemma
blocks.text: During a simulated audit, a consultant discovers that a client is hiding a personal data breach from its regulator. Rather than publishing the information on social media, the consultant documents it, informs the client's senior management in writing and reminds them of their notification obligations, then consults their own legal department on what to do next if nothing is done.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Compliance officer: I report to senior management on the status of obligations.
Executive: I can be held personally liable if I neglect security.
Auditor: I stay independent and report what I find, even if it is uncomfortable.
Analyst: I never use my access for personal purposes.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Due care = act; due diligence = verify.
Negligence = not doing what a prudent person would have done.
An effective compliance program has a designated owner, audits and disciplinary rules.
Ethics: protect society first, stay legal, go through the proper channels.
Due care and due diligence; negligence; liability toward third parties.
Compliance program: owner, inventory, policies, training, audits, reporting, corrections.
Codes of ethics and unethical behavior.
Deciding: society, legality, honesty, proper channels.
